messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody. I want to compare different birdsong syllables using the cov.spectro function. For that I would like to have all sounds in a specific frequency range, or in other words "allign the frequency" (eg. minimum frequency set at 5000Hz for all sounds). This is to avoid low correlation values due to differences in the frequency range of the sounds, and focusing on comparing the "shape" of the sound. Which brings up my question: I would like to know if there is a way of fixing the frequency of a sound to a desired value. I thought about using the synth2 function which allows you to create a new sound based on the original one. I have been able to recover the original sound and shift its frequency. But it would save me a lot of time if I could, instead of "shifting the frequency by 1000Hz", command at WHICH frequency I want the sound to be.  I hope I made myself clear enough.
Thank you in advance for your help

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andres,

This is a tough question because there is no single defined "frequency" to most sounds. For instance, if you look at the spectrogram for the orni data used in the example for lfs(), you can see that the energy is distributed at lots of different frequencies, with most of it concentrated between 4 and 6 kHz. There is no well-defined pitch for this sound.

If your sound is tonal, with a reasonably small variation in pitch, you might be able to use dfreq() to extract that pitch programmatically, and use it to automate your calls to lfs(). E.g., say you wanted to take the peewit data, wihch is roughly 1 kHz, and shift it to 2 kHz:

data(peewit)
spectro(peewit)
peewit_pitch = dfreq(peewit)
peewit_2k = lfs(peewit, 22050, (2 - median(peewit_pitch[, 2])) * 1000)
spectro(peewit_2k, 22050)

best,
jesse

messages.body_plain:
Reading your question more carefully, I noticed that you were using synth2(), which is an awesome function I hadn't played with! Here's an alternative method using synth2():

data(peewit)
env.peewit <- env(peewit, f=22050, plot=FALSE)
ifreq.peewit <- ifreq(peewit, f=22050, plot=FALSE)$f[,2]
ifreq.peewit.shifted = ifreq.peewit + (3 - mean(ifreq.peewit))
peewit_3k = synth2(env=env.peewit, ifreq=1000 * ifreq.peewit.shifted, f=22050, plot=TRUE)

Note that in either of these approaches, the choice of how to describe the frequency of the original signal is not obvious.  I used median() in the first, and mean() in the second, but those aren't necessarily well motivated :)

best,
jesse

Hi Andrés,

I also see distortion with lfs(). You might be able to mitigate this some by playing with the fft window length.

The ifreq() method seems to work a lot better for tico, but not very well for a sound with harmonics like peewit. Both this technique and the lfs() technique are transforming the sounds to a different domain (spectrogram or Hilbert transform) and losing some information, so it's not surprising that the resulting sounds would have some distortion!

I'm afraid I don't know a way to keep this from happening. I've noticed that artifacts can be introduced when I pitch-shift using other tools such as Audacity, as well.

I wonder if you might be best off avoiding pitch-shifting altogether, treating the spectrograms as matrices directly and calculating the correlation between the spectrograms incorporating both a time shift (as in covspectro) and a frequency shift (as in corspec).

best,
jesse

Hi Jesse,
when I use the synth2 function I don't see the distortion, actually the spectrogram at least looks identical.

After exploring a bit more I think using the median is pretty good because you can set the center of each syllable at a certain frequency. The syllables I'm working with (Timberline wren) are pretty similar to the ones in tico, although the forms are more variable and complex. The great majority of them don't have harmonics, so the ifreq works pretty well.

I've also thought about calculating the correlation incorporating time and frequency shift although I don't have any idea of how to do it in R. The Raven correlator doesn't do frequency shifting, only time. I read in the Avisoft manual that the correlator does both time and frequency shifting, but getting a licence for avisoft, can be expensive and complicated.

Thank you again for your help and feedback I appreciate it very much.
Best,

Andrés

Betreff: Re: [seewave] Relative amplitude not adequate shown

Hi Martin,

I'm not 100% sure what is going on, but I suspect that your file is being normalized before or during the pastew() function. There might be a way to stop that, but I'm not sure exactly how to. Possibly, you might consider looking at the non-normalized amplitude envelope: env(..., norm = F), but that's just a guess.

A work around would be to use the command line program "SoX" to concatenate the files together before comparing them with oscillo() or spectro().  Make sure you have Sox installed (http://sox.sourceforge.net/) and you can call it from R using the sox() function.

To concatenate (or paste together in sequence) your wave files use the following command:

sox("frog1.wav frog2.wav frog3.wav threecalls.wav")  ##this pastes them together into a new wave and saves it to the working directory
calls <- readWave("threecalls.wav")  ##Open the new wave file
oscillo(calls)

Alternatively you could combine them with Audacity, but this could be time consuming if you have a lot to do.

Good luck,

Steffi

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ross,

I use seewave for all of those measurements, with the possible exception of the "number of calls in a recording" because seewave is a bit slow when dealing with really large files (mine are all > 30 min).

I use a series of R scripts to extract these measures. First I manually specify the start and stop times of all notes (I work with chickadee songs), then I have R + seewave calculate note/song lengths. Next I'd use dfreq() to calculate dominant frequencies measured at different times across the note and use these numbers to get the freq at the start and stop of the note. You could also use this to get the maximum freq and the corresponding time of that freq (but that would be the maximum dominant freq, which may not be what you want. You could also use spec() and manually select the maximum freq from the power spectrum). From dfreq() you could also get the freq range by going from the minimum value to the maximum, but, once again, this somewhat depends on what kind of maximum frequency you want to measure.

Bear in mind that if you're unfamiliar with R, seewave can be a bit challenging at first so you should plan on some time invested to get things figured out. But once you've invested the time, it's amazing how automated you can make everything! Right now I use seewave to cut out my songs from the recording (through SoX), manually record the length of each note, and then automatically record frequency, and relative amplitude of all notes. I even have it set up to print out a series of spectrograms with the measurements drawn on them so I can verify that everything is measured correctly.

If you really get into the programming, you can even take advantage of multicore processing to speed things up, somewhat :)

I've also found seewave extremely useful for measurements.

One comment on some of the measurements of energy and duration: measurements can be made more precise and repeatable if you look at something like the inner 90% quantile of the energy distribution. In the case of energy, this can also help with "edge" effects, where the frequency given by dfreq() may not be part of the signal.

For more detail on this phenomenon see http://www.birds.cornell.edu/brp/research/algorithm/automated-and-robust-measurement-of-signal-features

I mention this because Raven has built-in facilities for doing measurements in this robust way, and seewave doesn't. That's the only difference I can think of. I personally choose seewave whenever I can, due to the convenience of being able to script it!

best,
jesse

Hi Steffi,

dfreq() seems to me to work pretty well even on somewhat noisy recordings. But you could have a version of it which only looked at the inner 90% of the energy per time slice, and that might help it be a little more robust in noisy situations.

I think what Cortopassi is actually suggesting is creating an aggregate power distribution as a function of frequency for the entire frequency band of interest, taking the inner 90% or so of the energy, and then computing measures such as mean, standard deviation, skewness, etc. on this distribution. These would be single measures, rather than vectors as we get from dfreq(), and they ought to be fairly robust to small variations in where the frequency band of interest is specified to be, which seem to be kind of inevitable when drawing boxes on spectrograms.

The approach has been coded up in a MATLAB toolkit called Acoustat, which has shown up in some publications. I believe the approach was originated by Kurt Fristrup. So those might be good google terms if you want to dig in further. I do not know what the licensing situation is with Acoustat, but if anybody is interested in porting the core algorithms to R/seewave, I could probably put them in touch with someone who would know about that.

Best,

Bioacoustics Research Program
Cornell Lab of Ornithology

I seem to remember you mentioned that you have Raven Pro? I actually find it very efficient to do this sort of thing in Raven, by drawing boxes.

In seewave, the best way would probably be to use the locator() function, which records the locations of mouse clicks. You'd just do locator(4), and then click on the points which represent the begin time, end time, high freq, and low freq. Then grab the numbers out of the resulting vector, and get the duration by subtracting begin time from end time.

Hi Jesse

Many thanks for taking time to respond.

My main motivation for switching to seewave and ditching Raven was to make the process of taking measurements both automated and reproducible. Making selections in Raven or using locator() in seewave IMO remove both automation and reproducibility.

I'm wondering if a workflow like this is possible:

1. open a wave file that contains Chiffchaff calls
2. delete portion of wave file outside the frequency range of a Chiffchaff call (<3khz and >4.5khz).
3. locate portion of the remaining wave file that contain sound above a certain amplitude
4. cut the wave file into separate wave files, each part containing sound above a certain amplitude
5. delete any cut wave files that are not Chiffchaff calls by either listening to files or plotting them
6. make a function that collects measurements from each wave file

This workflow might well appear strange or might not be possible. Basically I'm after a workflow that removes the need to make selections that cannot be reproduced at a later stage.

Cheers
Ross

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ross,

Glad to see you're jumping onto the seewave bandwagon :)

Depending on how long your wave files are, you might run into problems with seewave being a bit slow.  If, for example, you're like me and have ~20min recording files, then I would suggest looking into SoX for the first round of cutting and filtering (you can call SoX from seewave/R, making it really nice for integration) .

With respect to cutting out sounds above a certain amplitude I think you might be able to also use SoX for that as well. You can definitely use seewave for that, if your files are short, but I think you might run into long processing times if they're long.

As for using locator(), I would disagree that you loose reproducibility, at least within your project. You do gain some subjectivity, so I guess that's a loss of some reproducibility between observers. In my case, I use locator() to get the start and stop times of all notes. These times are saved as part of my dataset, so I can always go back and see what I defined the start and stop time to be and make changes to what measurements I want to extract. I spent a lot of time trying to get seewave/R to automatically select the start/stop times for me, but found that I was constantly having to correct it. In the end it was quicker for me to accept a bit of subjectivity on my part.

If you want something that is less subjective, then maybe you'd be interested in the processes that Jesse pointed out last week (with the aggregate power functions?), I think Jerome is implementing them for a future version of seewave. That way you could always define the start of your notes the same way. But, once again, you'd have to be aware of possible interference from background noises, and would probably have to do some quality checking, depending on how crucial that is to you.

Hope this helps,

Steffi
